name: PHAT

lead: PHAT is a lifting program created by Layne Norton, a natural bodybuilder and powerlifter with a PhD in nutritional sciences. It combines heavy low-rep training with higher-rep bodybuilding work so each muscle is trained twice a week in different ways.
People use it to add muscle size and strength, which changes shoulders, back, chest, arms and legs, the physique side of appearance.

paras: The standard week has an upper-body power day, a lower-body power day, then back and shoulder, lower-body, and chest and arms hypertrophy days, with two rest days. Power days use heavy compounds at low reps with long rests; hypertrophy days use moderate to high reps with shorter rests [2][3].

Sources describe it as demanding, with sessions of 75 to 120 minutes and roughly 8 to 12 hours a week, and advise against it for beginners or those with limited gym access or recovery [2][3]. Overuse injury is the main practical risk of high-volume training.

chain: More muscle size across the body
angle.text: PHAT is a structured way to gain muscle, which improves shoulders, back, chest, arms and legs, so the visual benefit is a more muscular physique.

lead: PHAT, short for Power Hypertrophy Adaptive Training, is a five-day powerbuilding split created and popularized by Layne Norton, a natural bodybuilder and powerlifter with a doctorate in nutritional sciences [1][2]. It blends strength-focused and size-focused training in one week: two heavy 'power' days followed by three higher-volume 'hypertrophy' days, with each muscle group trained twice [1][3].

People use PHAT to build muscle mass and strength, which shows up as broader shoulders, a thicker back, fuller chest and arms and larger legs. Training each muscle twice per week, once with heavy loads and once with higher volume, is aimed at a bigger, more developed physique [1][3]. Publications describe it as built for intermediate lifters who have a basic strength base and a well-equipped gym [1][3].

The program circulates on looksmax.org, where a thread presents it as a gym program for thin lifters [4]. Studies of resistance training generally examine training frequency and volume rather than this named program; a 2016 meta-analysis of frequency found a larger effect size for higher-frequency training than lower [5].
infobox: Five per week, two rest days [1]

paras: PHAT was designed by Layne Norton, who was born in Evansville, Indiana, holds a bachelor's degree in biochemistry and a PhD in nutritional sciences, and runs the coaching and nutrition brand Biolayne and a supplement line, according to a biographical profile [2]. The profile lists natural bodybuilding wins from 2001 onwards, including a pro-level win in 2010, and raw powerlifting titles from 2009, including a silver medal at the 2015 IPF World Championships in the 93 kg class [2]. BarBend notes that he has competed in powerlifting since 2009 and placed second at the 2015 IPF World Classic Championships [3].

The program's appeal rests on that dual background: it fuses the heavy, low-repetition work typical of powerlifting with the higher-repetition, isolation-heavy work of bodybuilding, a style often called powerbuilding [1]. An exercise-tracking app description places the original publication on the SimplyShredded website in 2011.

The standard template is upper power, lower power, rest, back and shoulders hypertrophy, lower hypertrophy, chest and arms hypertrophy, rest [1][3]. Called a five-day split, the layout contains five training days in the week with two rest days, and the rest days can be moved to suit a schedule [1].

Power days use heavy compound lifts, about 3-5 sets of 3-5 reps with long rests of several minutes; accessory movements on those days use about 6-10 reps. On the upper power day StrengthLog lists barbell rows, pull-ups, lat pulldowns, dumbbell presses, dips, shoulder presses and arm work; the lower power day centres on squats, hack squats, stiff-legged deadlifts, leg curls and calf raises [1].

Hypertrophy days use about 6-20 reps, with speed work first on lighter loads at roughly 85% of the power-day weight, shorter rests of about 1-3 minutes and more isolation work such as lateral raises, curls and triceps extensions [1][3]. BarBend describes the hypertrophy sets as stopping one to two reps short of failure and the speed sets as lighter loads moved quickly [3]. Progression is described as adding small increments once all sets reach the top of the rep range, rotating exercise variations when lifts stall, then deloading [1][3].

StrengthLog describes a four-day version that merges the two upper-body hypertrophy days into one, reducing volume by roughly 30-40%, and notes that exercises can be swapped, for example deadlifts for squats or a barbell bench for dumbbell presses [1]. The program contains no direct ab work, and the same source suggests adding a few sets of ab exercises to a couple of hypertrophy sessions [1].

The same article says PHAT can be run during a diet with lighter speed sets and possibly fewer accessories, though progress is likely to be slower, and suggests a deload every 6-12 weeks at roughly 60-70% of normal loads [1]. Related named programs such as PHUL (four days per week, lower volume) and PH3 (strength-focused around the three main lifts) are separate templates [1].

Reviewers describe PHAT as not a beginner program and as needing a well-equipped gym, substantial time and good recovery [1][3]. BarBend estimates 8-12 hours per week in the weight room and notes that load prescriptions become less specific later in the program, so lifters choose weights themselves [3]. Limited direct ab work and slower progress while dieting are noted as drawbacks [1].

StrengthLog, which promotes its own training app, positions PHAT as demanding on sleep and nutrition and says the five-day schedule can strain social life [1]. BarBend names intermediate lifters, off-season powerlifters and bodybuilders wanting leg development as the groups it suits, and home-gym users without machines and cables as the group it suits least [3].

No controlled trial has compared PHAT as a named program against other routines. The research relevant to its design concerns training frequency and volume. A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger identified ten studies of resistance-training frequency and reported that higher frequency was associated with a greater effect size than lower frequency (about 0.49 versus 0.30) [5]. The authors could not produce reliable estimates for studies where total volume was matched, because of limited sample sizes [5].

These findings are often cited in discussion of why splitting heavy and high-volume work across two sessions per muscle is workable; PHAT's specific mix of low-rep power work and higher-rep hypertrophy work has not been isolated in trials.

A looksmax.org thread recommends PHAT to skinny members seeking to gain size [4]. In looksmaxxing terms, gaining muscle is part of 'bodymaxxing', which addresses shoulder width, back thickness and overall frame to complement facial improvements. Norton's program is also referenced on T Nation training logs, where lifters report following it after other routines.
No studies found of PHAT itself. Reviews of resistance training study volume and frequency, not this named program [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org PHAT is recommended as a mass-building routine for thin lifters, and on T Nation it appears in logs as an option after other programs [4].

claims.claim: PHAT is a good routine for skinny lifters to gain size
Training each muscle twice a week with heavy and high-volume sessions builds more muscle
PHAT can be adapted to four days or run during a diet
The program needs a well-equipped gym and substantial time

Norton's original PHAT program published on SimplyShredded, according to a program-tracking app description.

Norton takes silver at the IPF World Championships in the 93 kg class [3][2].
Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger publish a meta-analysis of resistance-training frequency and hypertrophy [5].
